https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Plante & Moran's management letter on the June 30, 2024 audit, dated October 28, 2024 — a clean report with a single recommendation. The only finding is that the Food Service Fund balance still exceeds the USDA's three-month maximum. Two figures stand out: the district recorded an **arbitrage liability of $3,693,631** on unspent bond proceeds, and its fund balance of 19.21% — about ten weeks of operations — sits below the 21.86% statewide average.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
The auditor's Report to the Board of Education for the year ended June 30, 2024, from Plante & Moran, PLLC — Chris Geck, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Senior Manager) — dated October 28, 2024. Three sections: Results of the Audit, Other Recommendations and Observations, and Informational Items. The engagement letter is dated June 17, 2024 and the planning meeting was August 27, 2024.

Results of the audit — clean
No new accounting policies adopted and no changes in application. No transactions lacking authoritative guidance. No transactions recognized in a different period than they occurred. **No difficulties encountered. No disagreements with management. All identified misstatements corrected by management.** No consultations with other accountants. Disclosures described as neutral, consistent and clear.

The most sensitive estimates are the district's share of MPSERS: a **$288.9 million net pension liability** and a **$4.9 million net OPEB asset** at June 30, 2024, per Office of Retirement Services data.

The one recommendation
The Food Service Fund balance continues to exceed the USDA's maximum allowance of three months' operating expenditures. The district should continue to monitor its spenddown plan entered into with the Michigan Department of Education.

Fund balance in context
General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by about $4.2 million in 2023/24, taking fund balance to approximately **$36.8 million** at June 30, 2024. The district's fund balance percentage is **19.21%, roughly 10 weeks of operations**, against a statewide average at June 30, 2023 of **21.86%, roughly 11 weeks**.

Arbitrage
With unspent bond proceeds accruing investment earnings, the district completed its analysis and determined an **arbitrage liability of $3,693,631**, reported in the government-wide statement of net position at June 30, 2024.

School funding, in depth
2023/24 raised the target foundation allowance $458 to $9,608, a 5% increase, with hold-harmless districts receiving the same increase and cyber schools held at $9,150. MPSERS total contribution rose to 48% of payroll from 45%, with the district's net cost rising from 28% to about 31% — the first increase in several years.

**2024/25 provided no foundation allowance increase at all.** Instead, revisions to Section 147 retirement categoricals free up roughly **$400 per pupil**, though not every district realizes the full amount. Every pre-conference version of the bill had carried a foundation increase of $217 to $302 per pupil. The OPEB plan is now considered fully funded; of about $669 million of statewide historical OPEB UAAL support, the bill redirects **$598 million** back to districts through categorical 147a4, about 5.75% of MPSERS payroll. Mental health and school safety took the most significant funding reduction. At-risk funding now exceeds $1 billion.

Under Section 30d the district received **$3,676,677** in state funding for universal free meals in 2023/24.

MPSERS statewide
Net pension liability fell about 15% to **$32.4 billion** at September 30, 2023 from $37.9 billion. The OPEB portion **flipped from a $2.1 billion net liability to a $566 million net asset** — driven by an 8.3% investment return against a 4.8% loss the prior year.

What's coming
GASB 101 (compensated absences) and GASB 102 (risk disclosures) effective June 30, 2025; GASB 103 (reporting model) June 30, 2026. Sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 lets millages approved after May 7, 2023 fund student transportation vehicles, with three separate accounting cohorts required. Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1 supersedes Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4 for June 30, 2024 reporting. OMB's April 2024 Uniform Guidance revisions raise the single audit threshold from $750,000 to $1 million and the equipment capitalization threshold from $5,000 to $10,000.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is the Report to the Board of Education prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC following the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2024. It is signed by Chris Geck, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager, and dated October 28, 2024 — the same date as the audit report itself. The letter thanks Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan and the business office for their assistance and preparedness. It is organized into Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (5-6), and Informational Items (7-19).

**Results of the audit.** The auditors set out their responsibility under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards per the engagement letter dated June 17, 2024: to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management with Board oversight are fairly presented in all material respects, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance that they are free of material misstatement. They considered internal control solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on it. The audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General, with a separate letter of the same date covering internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing. The audit followed the scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting of August 27, 2024.

The significant findings are uniformly clean. No new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies did not change during 2024. No transactions were entered into for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus. No significant transactions were recognized in a different period than when they occurred. No significant difficulties were encountered in performing and completing the audit. There were no disagreements with management. Management corrected all known and likely misstatements identified other than trivial ones. There were no consultations with other independent accountants. The disclosures in the financial statements are described as neutral, consistent and clear. On other information included in annual reports, the auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to their attention suggesting it was materially misstated or materially inconsistent with the financial statements.

The most sensitive accounting estimates are identified as the district's share of the MPSERS net liability for the pension plan and net asset for the other postemployment benefit plans, recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statements 68 and 75. The district's estimates as of June 30, 2024 were **$288.9 million for the pension plan and $4.9 million for the OPEB plan**, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. The auditors evaluated the key factors and assumptions and determined them reasonable in relation to the financial statements taken as a whole.

**Other recommendations and observations** contains exactly one item. The fund balance of the Food Service Fund continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures, and the district should continue to monitor its spenddown plan, entered into with the Michigan Department of Education, for reducing the balance to an acceptable level. The same paragraph is repeated verbatim in the Informational Items section.

**Informational items** run to thirteen pages and are largely sector commentary rather than district-specific findings, but several passages carry figures specific to Troy.

On the changing financial resources landscape, the auditors note that beginning with the 2024/2025 school aid budget they observed a change in budget strategy, with projections suggesting slowing growth for the School Aid Fund. For the first time in several years the governor and Legislature faced difficult choices about what to fund or cut, including evaluating initiatives borne out of the pandemic. While the School Aid Fund is as large as it has ever been, spreading funding to all desired initiatives is no longer realistic.

On 2023/2024 state funding, the May 2023 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference identified significant new resources. Key highlights: the target foundation allowance rose $458 per pupil to $9,608, a 5 percent increase, with hold-harmless districts receiving the same increase and cyber schools remaining at $9,150. The traditional blended pupil count continued at 90 percent October 2023 and 10 percent February 2023, with a new provision allowing declining-enrollment districts a two-year blended count funded through Section 29. Special education funding became fully categorical under Section 51 rather than drawing on the foundation allowance under Section 20. MPSERS costs rose — the overall contribution rate increased to 48 percent of payroll from 45 percent, with the net cost to the district rising from 28 percent to approximately 31 percent, the first increase in several years. GSRP reimbursement was raised to the target foundation allowance level with higher income limits. Section 31a at-risk funding increased with an opportunity index weighting. Section 30d provided universal free breakfast and lunch. Additional transportation funding used a riders-per-square-mile formula. One-time infusions covered mental health and school safety and a student loan repayment program, the latter arriving late enough in the year to create revenue recognition challenges at June 30, 2024. ISD operations rose 5 percent to mirror the foundation increase.

On 2024/2025 state funding, the May 2024 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference predicted sufficient resources for current programs but slower growth, closer to pre-pandemic levels. The School Aid Bill **provided no foundation allowance increase** — the target stays at $9,608 per pupil. Instead, revisions to Section 147 MPSERS categoricals increase retirement funding, and analysis of the bill indicates the modifications free up about **$400 per pupil** for operations, though not every district realizes the full benefit. The letter notes pointedly that the revision was crafted in conference committee, and that every version of the bill before the conference report had provided a foundation allowance increase ranging from **$217 to $302 per pupil**.

On MPSERS OPEB, the plan is now considered fully funded, with sufficient assets to cover accrued health benefits for current and former employees' past service. State funding contributes to districts to cover UAAL costs of about **$669 million statewide** for the historical OPEB UAAL, and the 2024/2025 bill redirects **$598 million** of the savings back to districts through categorical **147a4**, representing approximately **5.75 percent of MPSERS-related payroll**. GSRP eligibility expanded to families under four times the federal poverty level. At-risk funding now exceeds **$1 billion** with new flexibility provisions. Transportation, Future Educator Fellowship, Student Teacher Stipend and ISD Operations continued without substantive change. Many smaller categoricals were eliminated or reduced, with the most significant reduction being mental health and school safety — not counted as a cut because it was a one-time program, but leaving districts that built programming around it to find other sources. The Headlee obligation continues to be funded from the special education allocation rather than partly from the foundation allowance.

Looking forward, the May 2024 conference indicated funding levels are levelling off, making it unlikely the School Aid Fund can sustain recent growth. Because many recently added categoricals were labelled one-time, they appear most at risk. The letter lists the challenges districts face: the impact of a recession; fully utilizing ARP ESSER III, which sunset September 30, 2024 — the "funding cliff" requiring each district to evaluate whether those resources supported recurring operations; staff retention and recruitment; attracting and retaining students; pupil count trends; evaluating learning-loss programs once pandemic funding ends; planning for expanded GSRP; assessing food service in the second year of state-funded free meals; staffing cost increases; inflation; technology costs; school security and mental health costs given the 2024/2025 reduction; and retirement system cost trends. On enrollment, statewide figures have historically been slightly under 1.5 million students, declining about 10,000 per year pre-pandemic but falling in excess of 50,000 during it, with current data suggesting only partial recovery. The letter observes that on average it takes about ten students to fully fund a teacher position.

On Michigan School Meals, free breakfast and lunch has been available to all students since 2023/2024. **Troy received $3,676,677 in Section 30d state funding for 2023/2024.** The revenue supports the Food Service Fund and replaces revenue previously received from student-paid meals. Eligibility requires participating in the National School Lunch Program, serving breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade, adopting the Community Eligibility Provision to maximize federal reimbursement, collecting family income information, and writing off all outstanding student negative balances — with the write-off funded from outside the Food Service Fund, since that fund is not allowed to absorb it. The letter notes many districts are experiencing Food Service fund balances beyond state limitations and must maintain spenddown plans.

On grants management, the winding down of ESSER, GEER and CRF has brought increased federal and state oversight and heightened focus on internal controls. The auditors suggest performing a risk assessment of key processes and controls as the district moves into fiscal 2025.

On MPSERS statewide, at September 30, 2023 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately **$32.4 billion**, a decrease of about 15 percent from **$37.9 billion** at September 30, 2022. The retiree health care portion had a **net OPEB asset of approximately $566 million** compared to a net OPEB liability of **$2.1 billion** the prior year — described as a significant milestone, flipping from net liability to net asset. Both movements are attributed primarily to investment returns: an 8.3 percent annual return for the year ended September 30, 2023 against a 4.8 percent loss the prior year.

On fund balance, the letter explains its importance for navigating unexpected losses or revenue shortfalls, avoiding cash flow borrowing, supporting credit ratings and enabling long-term planning. It records that during 2023/2024 General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately **$4.2 million**, increasing fund balance to approximately **$36.8 million** at June 30, 2024. Against a statewide average at June 30, 2023 of approximately **21.86 percent** of expenditures and outgoing transfers — equal to roughly 11 weeks of operating costs — **Troy's fund balance percentage is 19.21 percent, equal to approximately 10 weeks of operation.**

On upcoming pronouncements: GASB Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences, effective for the year ending June 30, 2025, requiring a liability in the full accrual statements for leave attributable to services already rendered that accumulates and is more likely than not to be used or paid, measured at each employee's pay rate at the statement date, while removing the gross additions/reductions disclosure and the liquidating-fund disclosure. GASB Statement No. 102, Certain Risk Disclosures, also effective June 30, 2025, requiring disclosure of concentrations or constraints, related events that could have substantial impact, and mitigating actions. GASB Statement No. 103, Financial Reporting Model Improvements, effective June 30, 2026, limiting MD&A to five topics, defining operating and nonoperating revenue and expense for proprietary funds with a new subtotal for operating income and noncapital subsidies, moving budgetary comparisons to required supplementary information, requiring separate presentation of major component unit information, and prescribing presentation of unusual or infrequent items.

On sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023, a sinking fund millage approved by voters after May 7, 2023 may now be used for acquisition of student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies and equipment, and for trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code used in building maintenance. Sinking funds authorized prior to March 29, 2017; between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023; and after May 7, 2023 must each be accounted for separately with their own balance sheet and statement of revenue, expenditures and changes in fund balance. A district levying a sinking fund must have an independent audit conducted annually including a review of uses.

On Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1, which supersedes Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4 and takes effect for June 30, 2024 sinking fund and bond compliance audits: districts no longer submit financial information on bond closeout, instead filing an annual transmittal letter on the status of the bond-funded Capital Projects Fund; the completion date is simplified to the June 30 immediately following the later of the certificate of substantial completion or 95 percent of bond proceeds being spent; multiple series approved by electors at the same time may be accounted for in one fund; and sinking fund levies renewed after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for in a capital projects fund separate from any remaining balance from earlier levies. Plante & Moran participated in reviewing and providing feedback on the new guidance.

On arbitrage, defined as the difference between the interest expense paid by the issuer and the earnings on invested bond proceeds, the letter notes school districts are tax-exempt and therefore subject to federal arbitrage compliance rules limiting retainable investment earnings, with a computation generally completed at the five-year anniversary of the original bond sale. **The district completed its analysis and determined an arbitrage liability of $3,693,631, reported as a liability in the government-wide statement of net position at June 30, 2024.**

Remaining items cover the Inflation Reduction Act — $369 billion over ten years to reduce emissions by approximately 40 percent by 2030, with a direct-payment option for tax-exempt entities covering qualifying capital improvements such as electric vehicles and renewable energy equipment, with credits available through 2032; OMB's April 2024 Uniform Guidance revisions raising the single audit and Type A thresholds from $750,000 to $1 million effective for the district's June 30, 2026 year end, and raising the equipment capitalization threshold from $5,000 to $10,000; cyber threats, noting education is among the top ransomware targets and referencing the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021; and firm service offerings on operations review and controls assessment, IT assessment and planning, and data analytics.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: WeatherTech Consulting Group's contractor recommendation for the 2025 districtwide roof program, dated November 11, 2024. Nine bids were opened; the recommendation splits the award between Royal Roofing for Baker Middle School ($607,900) and Troy Union Elementary ($537,900) and Division 7 Building Contractors for the Service Building ($88,922) — $1,234,722 in total, each award going to the low bidder.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
A transmittal dated 11-11-24 from Ann Crippen of WeatherTech Consulting Group, Inc. (7747 Auburn Road, Utica, MI 48317) to Rob Carson at Troy School District, copied to Katelyn Magierka and Mark Paulus at TSD and John McCaig at WeatherTech, recommending contractor awards for Bid No. 2425-02, the Troy School District 2025 Roof Program.

The process
A non-mandatory pre-bid conference was held 10/25/24 with **eight bidders attending**; on 11/5/24 **nine electronic bids** were submitted and read aloud. No exclusions or qualifications were submitted. WeatherTech interviewed Royal Roofing and Division 7 Building Contractors to review qualifications, schedules and bid quantities, and concluded on the basis of the bid documents, submitted bids, post-bid submittals and interviews that the two provide the best value.

The awards
| Scope | Contractor | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Baker Middle School — Roof Areas B, E and Front Entrance Canopy | Royal Roofing | $607,900 |
| Troy Union Elementary — Roof Area F | Royal Roofing | $537,900 |
| Service Building — Roof Area C | Division 7 Building Contractors | $88,922 |
| **Total** | | **$1,234,722** |

Manufacturers are TBD for Baker and the Service Building; Elevate or Carlisle for Troy Union.

The bid comparison
Nine firms bid: Bloom Roofing Systems, Division 7 Building Contractors, JD Candler Roofing, KJP Roofing & Sheet Metal, Newton Crane Roofing, Quality Roofing, Royal Roofing, Royal West Roofing and Sheet Metal, and Schena Roofing & Sheet Metal.

On Baker Middle School, Royal Roofing was low at $607,900 ($16.56/sq ft over 36,700 sq ft), against JD Candler $619,300, Quality $659,075, Newton Crane $668,000, Division 7 $671,383, Schena $679,000, Bloom $720,347 and KJP $977,000. Royal West did not bid. The spread from low to second is 2%.

On Troy Union Elementary, Royal Roofing was again low at $537,900 ($17.35/sq ft over 31,000 sq ft), against Quality $548,011, Newton Crane $557,000, JD Candler $579,800, Division 7 $584,300, Bloom $589,972, Schena $661,000 and KJP $888,000 — a 1.88% spread to second.

On the Service Building, Division 7 was low at $88,922 ($18.22/sq ft over 4,880 sq ft), against Royal West $96,000, JD Candler $97,800, Bloom $104,021, Royal Roofing $110,900, Newton Crane $129,000, Schena $129,700, Quality $137,026 and KJP $197,000 — a 7.96% spread.

KJP Roofing bid highest on all three packages, at roughly 60% to 120% above the low bid in each case.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is the contractor bid recommendation for Bid No. 2425-02, the Troy School District 2025 Roof Program, submitted as a transmittal dated 11-11-24 by WeatherTech Consulting Group, Inc. WeatherTech's address is 7747 Auburn Road, Utica, MI 48317, telephone 586.731.3095, fax 586.731.6863, email weathertech@wtcg.net. The memorandum is from Ann Crippen to Rob Carson of Troy School District, copied to Katelyn Magierka and Mark Paulus at the district and John McCaig at WeatherTech. It appears at the November 12, 2024 meeting and again as agenda item 8.E. at a subsequent meeting.

The procurement history is set out briefly. A non-mandatory pre-bid conference was held on 10/25/24 and eight bidders attended. On 11/5/24 nine electronic bids were submitted and read aloud. No exclusions or qualifications were submitted with any bid. WeatherTech then conducted interviews with Royal Roofing and Division 7 Building Contractors to review their qualifications, schedules and bid quantities to complete the work. Based on the bid documents, the submitted bids, post-bid submittals and the post-bid interviews, WeatherTech concluded that Royal Roofing and Division 7 Building Contractors provide the best value to the district, and recommended that both be awarded contracts for the districtwide program.

The recommended awards cover three scopes. Royal Roofing is recommended for Baker Middle School — Roof Areas B, E and the Front Entrance Canopy — at a bid amount of **$607,900**, manufacturer to be determined; and for Troy Union Elementary — Roof Area F — at **$537,900**, with the manufacturer specified as Elevate or Carlisle. Division 7 Building Contractors is recommended for the Service Building — Roof Area C — at **$88,922**, manufacturer to be determined. The document's own summary lines read "Royal Roofing Total Bid: $537,900" and "Contractors Total Bid: $88,922," which reflect the extraction interleaving the two award blocks; the bid comparison sheet resolves the ambiguity, and the three scopes total **$1,234,722**, matching the "Total Low Bid Options" figure printed at the foot of the comparison sheet.

The attached bid comparison sheet records all nine bidders across the three packages: Bloom Roofing Systems Inc, Division 7 Building Contractors, JD Candler Roofing Company, KJP Roofing & Sheet Metal, Newton Crane Roofing Inc, Quality Roofing, Royal Roofing, Royal West Roofing and Sheet Metal, and Schena Roofing & Sheet Metal.

For Baker Middle School, Roof Areas B, E and the Front Entrance Canopy, the square footages bid range from 36,103 to 39,300, reflecting each contractor's own take-off. Bids were Bloom $720,347 on 37,861 sq ft ($19.03/sq ft, 30 work days); Division 7 $671,383 on 36,103 sq ft ($18.60, 25 days); JD Candler $619,300 on 37,300 sq ft ($16.60, 23 days); KJP $977,000 on 37,000 sq ft ($26.41, 23 days); Newton Crane $668,000 on 39,300 sq ft ($17.00, 20 days); Quality $659,075 on 36,400 sq ft ($18.11, 16 days); **Royal Roofing $607,900 on 36,700 sq ft ($16.56, 20 days)**; Royal West no bid; and Schena $679,000 on 36,103 sq ft ($18.81, 25 days). The sheet notes a delta of 1-2 and a 2% spread. Royal Roofing is both the lowest total and the lowest unit price.

For Troy Union Elementary, Roof Area F, square footages range from 31,000 to 32,000. Bids were Bloom $589,972 on 31,018 sq ft ($19.02, 25 days); Division 7 $584,300 on 31,284 sq ft ($18.68, 24 days); JD Candler $579,800 on 31,200 sq ft ($18.58, 26 days); KJP $888,000 on 31,500 sq ft ($28.19, 20 days); Newton Crane $557,000 on 31,800 sq ft ($17.52, 15 days); Quality $548,011 on 32,000 sq ft ($17.13, 14 days); **Royal Roofing $537,900 on 31,000 sq ft ($17.35, 18 days)**; Royal West no bid; and Schena $661,000 on 31,284 sq ft ($21.13, 30 days). The spread to second is 1.88%. Royal Roofing is lowest in total, though Quality Roofing's unit price of $17.13 is marginally lower — Royal's advantage comes from bidding the smallest area.

For the Service Building, Roof Area C, square footages range from 4,500 to 5,000. Bids were Bloom $104,021 on 4,500 sq ft ($23.12, 8 days); **Division 7 $88,922 on 4,880 sq ft ($18.22, 4 days)**; JD Candler $97,800 on 5,000 sq ft ($19.56, 5 days); KJP $197,000 on 5,000 sq ft ($39.40, 5 days); Newton Crane $129,000 on 4,700 sq ft ($27.45, 5 days); Quality $137,026 on 5,000 sq ft ($27.41, 5 days); Royal Roofing $110,900 on 4,880 sq ft ($22.73, 6 days); Royal West $96,000 on 5,000 sq ft ($19.20, 7 days); and Schena $129,700 on 4,880 sq ft ($26.58, 7 days). The spread is 7.96% — the widest of the three packages — and Division 7 is lowest on both total and unit price, with the shortest schedule at four work days.

The pattern across all three packages is that each award goes to the low bidder on its scope, so the recommendation is straightforward rather than a departure requiring justification. This is worth noting against the district's August 2025 general trades award, where the recommendation explicitly passed over the low bidder on performance grounds. KJP Roofing & Sheet Metal bid highest on every package — $977,000 against $607,900 at Baker, $888,000 against $537,900 at Troy Union, and $197,000 against $88,922 at the Service Building — between roughly 60% and 120% above the low bid in each case.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Unaudited statements through September 30, 2024 — three months into fiscal 2024-25 with still no state or federal revenue received. The General Fund shows a $(2,997,561) deficit on $24,542,391 of revenue against $27,539,952 of expenditure. The 2023 Capital Projects Fund has accelerated sharply, spending $13,115,317 of capital outlay in the quarter against $16.9 million for all of the prior year.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
Unaudited statements for July 1 – September 30, 2024, presented November 19, 2024. Three months in.

General Fund (3 of 12 months)
- Revenues $24,542,391 of $191,544,523 (12.8%) — Local $21,701,515; **State nil**; **Federal nil**; Interdistrict $2,840,876
- Expenditures $27,539,952 of $195,485,356 (14.1%) — Instruction $14,425,401; Support Services $13,031,377
- Result $(2,997,561) against a budgeted full-year $(3,940,833)

Three months into the year the district has received nothing from the state, which supplies 66% of budgeted revenue. Central Services at $1,491,623 has consumed 38% of its annual budget — the most front-loaded line.

Debt Service
Revenues $15,653,090 against expenditures of $650 — the summer levy accumulating against a $21,415,000 principal payment due in the spring. Surplus $15,652,440.

A posting anomaly worth noting
The Food Service Fund reports **identical figures to July and August** — revenue $116,685, expenditure $87,811, all component lines unchanged — for the third consecutive month. September is a full month of school meals, so this reflects a posting lag rather than genuine inactivity; the October statement records the catch-up.

Other funds
Troy Career Center: $851,926 balanced. Community Service: revenues $475,341 against expenditures $325,658, surplus $149,683. Preschool: revenues $434,474 against expenditures $510,612, swinging to a $(76,138) deficit as school-year staffing resumes with no state revenue yet received.

Capital funds
2023 Capital Projects: revenue $2,519,926 against expenditures of $13,218,246 — purchased services $99,555, capital outlay $13,115,317, outgoing transfers $3,375 — a $(10,698,320) draw. Capital outlay in this single quarter is 78% of the entire prior year's $16,854,191, marking a decisive acceleration in the bond program. Sinking Fund: revenue $2,457,194 against capital outlay $1,809,479, surplus $647,715. 2019 Capital Projects: revenue $15,896, no expenditure.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
These are Troy School District's unaudited statements for July 1 through September 30, 2024 — the first quarter of fiscal 2024-25 — presented to the Board on November 19, 2024. All funds report against the 6/20/24 adopted budget.

General Fund revenues total $24,542,391 against $191,544,523 budgeted, 12.8% of plan. By source: Local Sources $21,701,515 of $47,455,345 — 46%, as the summer levy settles; State Sources nil of $126,436,088; Federal Sources nil of $4,502,005; and Interdistrict Sources $2,840,876 of $13,151,085 — 22%. Three months into the fiscal year the district has still received nothing from the state, which accounts for 66% of budgeted revenue; the Michigan school aid payment cycle begins in October.

General Fund expenditures total $27,539,952 against $195,485,356, 14.1%. Instruction totals $14,425,401 against $128,084,453 — Basic Programs $10,848,552, Added Needs $3,467,142, Adult Education $109,707. Support Services total $13,031,377 against $66,585,319: Pupil $1,835,060; Instructional Staff $2,102,242; General Administration $531,600; School Administration $1,915,562; Business Services $462,859; Operations $3,698,473; Pupil Transportation $382,945; Central Services $1,491,623; Athletics and Other $611,013. Community Services $40,906 and Debt Service $42,268, with Outgoing Transfers nil.

The result is $(2,997,561) against a budgeted full-year $(3,940,833). Against the calendar, Central Services at $1,491,623 has consumed 38.5% of its $3,877,086 annual budget in a quarter — the most front-loaded line, reflecting annual technology, licensing and software costs. General Administration at 21% and Operations at 26% are also ahead. Pupil Transportation at $382,945 is 8.9% of budget, and Instruction overall at 11.3% is behind the calendar, as expected in a quarter containing the summer.

The Consolidated Debt Service Funds show revenues of $15,653,090 against $31,930,500 budgeted, all local with state nil against a $279,800 budget, against expenditures of just $650 in Other Transactions — principal of $21,415,000 and interest of $10,292,530 both untouched. The surplus is $15,652,440. The fund is accumulating the summer levy against a spring payment, exactly as it did the prior year.

The Food Service Fund reports figures identical to both the July and August statements: revenues $116,685 (Local $754, State nil, Federal $115,931, Interdistrict nil) against expenditures $87,811 (Salaries $6,370, Employee Benefits $487, Purchased Services $80,954, with supplies, capital outlay, other and transfers out all nil), for a surplus of $28,874. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Plante & Moran's management letter on the June 30, 2024 audit, dated October 28, 2024 — a clean report with a single recommendation. The only finding is that the Food Service Fund balance still exceeds the USDA's three-month maximum. Two figures stand out: the district recorded an **arbitrage liability of $3,693,631** on unspent bond proceeds, and its fund balance of 19.21% — about ten weeks of operations — sits below the 21.86% statewide average.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
What it is
The auditor's Report to the Board of Education for the year ended June 30, 2024, from Plante & Moran, PLLC — Chris Geck, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Senior Manager) — dated October 28, 2024. Three sections: Results of the Audit, Other Recommendations and Observations, and Informational Items. The engagement letter is dated June 17, 2024 and the planning meeting was August 27, 2024.

Results of the audit — clean
No new accounting policies adopted and no changes in application. No transactions lacking authoritative guidance. No transactions recognized in a different period than they occurred. **No difficulties encountered. No disagreements with management. All identified misstatements corrected by management.** No consultations with other accountants. Disclosures described as neutral, consistent and clear.

The most sensitive estimates are the district's share of MPSERS: a **$288.9 million net pension liability** and a **$4.9 million net OPEB asset** at June 30, 2024, per Office of Retirement Services data.

The one recommendation
The Food Service Fund balance continues to exceed the USDA's maximum allowance of three months' operating expenditures. The district should continue to monitor its spenddown plan entered into with the Michigan Department of Education.

Fund balance in context
General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by about $4.2 million in 2023/24, taking fund balance to approximately **$36.8 million** at June 30, 2024. The district's fund balance percentage is **19.21%, roughly 10 weeks of operations**, against a statewide average at June 30, 2023 of **21.86%, roughly 11 weeks**.

Arbitrage
With unspent bond proceeds accruing investment earnings, the district completed its analysis and determined an **arbitrage liability of $3,693,631**, reported in the government-wide statement of net position at June 30, 2024.

School funding, in depth
2023/24 raised the target foundation allowance $458 to $9,608, a 5% increase, with hold-harmless districts receiving the same increase and cyber schools held at $9,150. MPSERS total contribution rose to 48% of payroll from 45%, with the district's net cost rising from 28% to about 31% — the first increase in several years.

**2024/25 provided no foundation allowance increase at all.** Instead, revisions to Section 147 retirement categoricals free up roughly **$400 per pupil**, though not every district realizes the full amount. Every pre-conference version of the bill had carried a foundation increase of $217 to $302 per pupil. The OPEB plan is now considered fully funded; of about $669 million of statewide historical OPEB UAAL support, the bill redirects **$598 million** back to districts through categorical 147a4, about 5.75% of MPSERS payroll. Mental health and school safety took the most significant funding reduction. At-risk funding now exceeds $1 billion.

Under Section 30d the district received **$3,676,677** in state funding for universal free meals in 2023/24.

MPSERS statewide
Net pension liability fell about 15% to **$32.4 billion** at September 30, 2023 from $37.9 billion. The OPEB portion **flipped from a $2.1 billion net liability to a $566 million net asset** — driven by an 8.3% investment return against a 4.8% loss the prior year.

What's coming
GASB 101 (compensated absences) and GASB 102 (risk disclosures) effective June 30, 2025; GASB 103 (reporting model) June 30, 2026. Sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 lets millages approved after May 7, 2023 fund student transportation vehicles, with three separate accounting cohorts required. Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1 supersedes Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4 for June 30, 2024 reporting. OMB's April 2024 Uniform Guidance revisions raise the single audit threshold from $750,000 to $1 million and the equipment capitalization threshold from $5,000 to $10,000.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is the Report to the Board of Education prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC following the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2024. It is signed by Chris Geck, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager, and dated October 28, 2024 — the same date as the audit report itself. The letter thanks Mr. Dan Trudel, Mr. Aurel Malutan and the business office for their assistance and preparedness. It is organized into Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (5-6), and Informational Items (7-19).

**Results of the audit.** The auditors set out their responsibility under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards per the engagement letter dated June 17, 2024: to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management with Board oversight are fairly presented in all material respects, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance that they are free of material misstatement. They considered internal control solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on it. The audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General, with a separate letter of the same date covering internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing. The audit followed the scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting of August 27, 2024.

The significant findings are uniformly clean. No new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies did not change during 2024. No transactions were entered into for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus. No significant transactions were recognized in a different period than when they occurred. No significant difficulties were encountered in performing and completing the audit. There were no disagreements with management. Management corrected all known and likely misstatements identified other than trivial ones. There were no consultations with other independent accountants. The disclosures in the financial statements are described as neutral, consistent and clear. On other information included in annual reports, the auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to their attention suggesting it was materially misstated or materially inconsistent with the financial statements.

The most sensitive accounting estimates are identified as the district's share of the MPSERS net liability for the pension plan and net asset for the other postemployment benefit plans, recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statements 68 and 75. The district's estimates as of June 30, 2024 were **$288.9 million for the pension plan and $4.9 million for the OPEB plan**, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. The auditors evaluated the key factors and assumptions and determined them reasonable in relation to the financial statements taken as a whole.

**Other recommendations and observations** contains exactly one item. The fund balance of the Food Service Fund continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures, and the district should continue to monitor its spenddown plan, entered into with the Michigan Department of Education, for reducing the balance to an acceptable level. The same paragraph is repeated verbatim in the Informational Items section.

**Informational items** run to thirteen pages and are largely sector commentary rather than district-specific findings, but several passages carry figures specific to Troy.

On the changing financial resources landscape, the auditors note that beginning with the 2024/2025 school aid budget they observed a change in budget strategy, with projections suggesting slowing growth for the School Aid Fund. For the first time in several years the governor and Legislature faced difficult choices about what to fund or cut, including evaluating initiatives borne out of the pandemic. While the School Aid Fund is as large as it has ever been, spreading funding to all desired initiatives is no longer realistic.

On 2023/2024 state funding, the May 2023 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference identified significant new resources. Key highlights: the target foundation allowance rose $458 per pupil to $9,608, a 5 percent increase, with hold-harmless districts receiving the same increase and cyber schools remaining at $9,150. The traditional blended pupil count continued at 90 percent October 2023 and 10 percent February 2023, with a new provision allowing declining-enrollment districts a two-year blended count funded through Section 29. Special education funding became fully categorical under Section 51 rather than drawing on the foundation allowance under Section 20. MPSERS costs rose — the overall contribution rate increased to 48 percent of payroll from 45 percent, with the net cost to the district rising from 28 percent to approximately 31 percent, the first increase in several years. GSRP reimbursement was raised to the target foundation allowance level with higher income limits. Section 31a at-risk funding increased with an opportunity index weighting. Section 30d provided universal free breakfast and lunch. Additional transportation funding used a riders-per-square-mile formula. One-time infusions covered mental health and school safety and a student loan repayment program, the latter arriving late enough in the year to create revenue recognition challenges at June 30, 2024. ISD operations rose 5 percent to mirror the foundation increase.

On 2024/2025 state funding, the May 2024 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference predicted sufficient resources for current programs but slower growth, closer to pre-pandemic levels. The School Aid Bill **provided no foundation allowance increase** — the target stays at $9,608 per pupil. Instead, revisions to Section 147 MPSERS categoricals increase retirement funding, and analysis of the bill indicates the modifications free up about **$400 per pupil** for operations, though not every district realizes the full benefit. The letter notes pointedly that the revision was crafted in conference committee, and that every version of the bill before the conference report had provided a foundation allowance increase ranging from **$217 to $302 per pupil**.

On MPSERS OPEB, the plan is now considered fully funded, with sufficient assets to cover accrued health benefits for current and former employees' past service. State funding contributes to districts to cover UAAL costs of about **$669 million statewide** for the historical OPEB UAAL, and the 2024/2025 bill redirects **$598 million** of the savings back to districts through categorical **147a4**, representing approximately **5.75 percent of MPSERS-related payroll**. GSRP eligibility expanded to families under four times the federal poverty level. At-risk funding now exceeds **$1 billion** with new flexibility provisions. Transportation, Future Educator Fellowship, Student Teacher Stipend and ISD Operations continued without substantive change. Many smaller categoricals were eliminated or reduced, with the most significant reduction being mental health and school safety — not counted as a cut because it was a one-time program, but leaving districts that built programming around it to find other sources. The Headlee obligation continues to be funded from the special education allocation rather than partly from the foundation allowance.

Looking forward, the May 2024 conference indicated funding levels are levelling off, making it unlikely the School Aid Fund can sustain recent growth. Because many recently added categoricals were labelled one-time, they appear most at risk. The letter lists the challenges districts face: the impact of a recession; fully utilizing ARP ESSER III, which sunset September 30, 2024 — the "funding cliff" requiring each district to evaluate whether those resources supported recurring operations; staff retention and recruitment; attracting and retaining students; pupil count trends; evaluating learning-loss programs once pandemic funding ends; planning for expanded GSRP; assessing food service in the second year of state-funded free meals; staffing cost increases; inflation; technology costs; school security and mental health costs given the 2024/2025 reduction; and retirement system cost trends. On enrollment, statewide figures have historically been slightly under 1.5 million students, declining about 10,000 per year pre-pandemic but falling in excess of 50,000 during it, with current data suggesting only partial recovery. The letter observes that on average it takes about ten students to fully fund a teacher position.

On Michigan School Meals, free breakfast and lunch has been available to all students since 2023/2024. **Troy received $3,676,677 in Section 30d state funding for 2023/2024.** The revenue supports the Food Service Fund and replaces revenue previously received from student-paid meals. Eligibility requires participating in the National School Lunch Program, serving breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade, adopting the Community Eligibility Provision to maximize federal reimbursement, collecting family income information, and writing off all outstanding student negative balances — with the write-off funded from outside the Food Service Fund, since that fund is not allowed to absorb it. The letter notes many districts are experiencing Food Service fund balances beyond state limitations and must maintain spenddown plans.

On grants management, the winding down of ESSER, GEER and CRF has brought increased federal and state oversight and heightened focus on internal controls. The auditors suggest performing a risk assessment of key processes and controls as the district moves into fiscal 2025.

On MPSERS statewide, at September 30, 2023 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately **$32.4 billion**, a decrease of about 15 percent from **$37.9 billion** at September 30, 2022. The retiree health care portion had a **net OPEB asset of approximately $566 million** compared to a net OPEB liability of **$2.1 billion** the prior year — described as a significant milestone, flipping from net liability to net asset. Both movements are attributed primarily to investment returns: an 8.3 percent annual return for the year ended September 30, 2023 against a 4.8 percent loss the prior year.

On fund balance, the letter explains its importance for navigating unexpected losses or revenue shortfalls, avoiding cash flow borrowing, supporting credit ratings and enabling long-term planning. It records that during 2023/2024 General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately **$4.2 million**, increasing fund balance to approximately **$36.8 million** at June 30, 2024. Against a statewide average at June 30, 2023 of approximately **21.86 percent** of expenditures and outgoing transfers — equal to roughly 11 weeks of operating costs — **Troy's fund balance percentage is 19.21 percent, equal to approximately 10 weeks of operation.**

On upcoming pronouncements: GASB Statement No. 101, Compensated Absences, effective for the year ending June 30, 2025, requiring a liability in the full accrual statements for leave attributable to services already rendered that accumulates and is more likely than not to be used or paid, measured at each employee's pay rate at the statement date, while removing the gross additions/reductions disclosure and the liquidating-fund disclosure. GASB Statement No. 102, Certain Risk Disclosures, also effective June 30, 2025, requiring disclosure of concentrations or constraints, related events that could have substantial impact, and mitigating actions. GASB Statement No. 103, Financial Reporting Model Improvements, effective June 30, 2026, limiting MD&A to five topics, defining operating and nonoperating revenue and expense for proprietary funds with a new subtotal for operating income and noncapital subsidies, moving budgetary comparisons to required supplementary information, requiring separate presentation of major component unit information, and prescribing presentation of unusual or infrequent items.

On sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023, a sinking fund millage approved by voters after May 7, 2023 may now be used for acquisition of student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies and equipment, and for trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code used in building maintenance. Sinking funds authorized prior to March 29, 2017; between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023; and after May 7, 2023 must each be accounted for separately with their own balance sheet and statement of revenue, expenditures and changes in fund balance. A district levying a sinking fund must have an independent audit conducted annually including a review of uses.

On Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1, which supersedes Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4 and takes effect for June 30, 2024 sinking fund and bond compliance audits: districts no longer submit financial information on bond closeout, instead filing an annual transmittal letter on the status of the bond-funded Capital Projects Fund; the completion date is simplified to the June 30 immediately following the later of the certificate of substantial completion or 95 percent of bond proceeds being spent; multiple series approved by electors at the same time may be accounted for in one fund; and sinking fund levies renewed after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for in a capital projects fund separate from any remaining balance from earlier levies. Plante & Moran participated in reviewing and providing feedback on the new guidance.

On arbitrage, defined as the difference between the interest expense paid by the issuer and the earnings on invested bond proceeds, the letter notes school districts are tax-exempt and therefore subject to federal arbitrage compliance rules limiting retainable investment earnings, with a computation generally completed at the five-year anniversary of the original bond sale. **The district completed its analysis and determined an arbitrage liability of $3,693,631, reported as a liability in the government-wide statement of net position at June 30, 2024.**

Remaining items cover the Inflation Reduction Act — $369 billion over ten years to reduce emissions by approximately 40 percent by 2030, with a direct-payment option for tax-exempt entities covering qualifying capital improvements such as electric vehicles and renewable energy equipment, with credits available through 2032; OMB's April 2024 Uniform Guidance revisions raising the single audit and Type A thresholds from $750,000 to $1 million effective for the district's June 30, 2026 year end, and raising the equipment capitalization threshold from $5,000 to $10,000; cyber threats, noting education is among the top ransomware targets and referencing the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021; and firm service offerings on operations review and controls assessment, IT assessment and planning, and data analytics.
